title: Anand at dusk
hookLine: the six pauris also sit inside the evening Rehras

cards: Play a song you love at seven in the morning, on the way to work, coffee in hand. Then play the same song at seven in the evening, shoes off, lights low. It's the same recording, note for note.
But it isn't the same song. In the morning it pushes you out the door. In the evening it brings you home.
A Sikh who keeps the daily prayers meets the Anand twice a day, in two different lights.

teach.b: In the morning, the Rehat Maryada names the Japji, Jaap Sahib and the savaiyas, and many Sikhs add the whole Anand, all forty pauris, to those morning banis. That's the full meal.
Then evening comes, and with it Rehras, the evening prayer, which we'll walk through line by line starting in two days.

teach.h: DUSK: THE SIX PAURIS INSIDE REHRAS.
teach.b: Near its end, Rehras carries the same six pauris you now know: the first five, and the fortieth. So the Anand frames the day.
It's there at the start, in full, and it returns at dusk, shorter, like a taste of the morning's meal.

teach.h: THE SAME FIRST LINE AT BOTH ENDS.
teach.b: Think about what the first line sounds like at each end. Anand bhaiaa meree maae: joy has come, my mother, I have found the True Guru.
In the morning, that line goes out into the day ahead, before anything has gone right or wrong. At dusk, the day has happened. The bus was late.
Someone was unkind. Something good came out of nowhere. And still the same words come: joy has come, mother.
Not because the day was perfect.

teach.h: THE JOY: FROM THE GURU, NOT THE DAY.
teach.b: The line says where the joy comes from: I have found the True Guru. Not from the day. That's why it can be sung at both ends.
Some families sing the evening pauris together, standing in a kitchen, or sitting on the floor of a front room with the lamps just lit. Some say them alone on a train home. The words don't change.

how: Many Sikhs add the full Anand Sahib to their morning banis, and the evening Rehras Sahib includes its six pauris, the first five and the fortieth, before Ardas.

o: a bedtime song sung to children at dusk
a happy mood that comes after a good day
joy has come: the first words of the Anand

games.q: the day is ending and a family gathers for the evening prayer. where do the six pauris of the Anand come?
o: they're never said in the evening.
games.why: they sit inside Rehras, near its end, so the Anand frames the Sikh day at both ends.

practice: Look at the light outside, or if it isn't evening yet, picture the sky going orange.

Softly say or hum the first line two or three times, anand bhaiaa meree maae, satguroo mai paaiaa, joy has come, my mother, I have found the True Guru, and let your whole day so far, the good and the bad, stand behind the words.

wordCard.voice: Anand bhaiaa, joy has come. The six pauris of the Anand return inside Rehras, the evening prayer, so the song of bliss frames the Sikh day at both ends.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: anand bhaiaa, joy has come; the opening of the Anand, said in the morning and again at dusk.

carryVoice: Your line: dusk, with joy. The same words, whatever kind of day it was. Rest easy tonight.
